summary: Defines the Single Rate Three Color Marker, a meter used in Diffserv traffic conditioners. It measures a packet stream against a committed rate and burst allowances, then marks each packet green, yellow or red to show how well it conforms. Routers can then treat the colors differently. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: The srTCM measures IP packets against one committed rate and two burst sizes. It marks each packet green, yellow or red so later network equipment can apply different treatment.

subtitle: A two-bucket marker that colors IP packets according to a committed rate and burst sizes.

tldr.problem: A Diffserv traffic conditioner needs a way to compare packet traffic with a committed rate and burst allowances and mark packets that exceed them.
tldr.mechanism: The Single Rate Three Color Marker uses two token buckets that refill at one committed information rate. It marks packets green, yellow or red according to available tokens and, in Color-Aware mode, their prior color.
tldr.outcome: The Informational memo defines a meter and marker that can encode the result in the packet's DS field. It does not specify an Internet standard.

today: RFC 2697 is an Informational memo. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Marker Does
sections.content:
The Single Rate Three Color Marker (srTCM) is a component of a Differentiated Services traffic conditioner. Its Meter evaluates each IP packet and passes the result to a Marker, which records the color in the packet's DS field.

The three colors represent how a packet fits the Committed Burst Size (CBS) and Excess Burst Size (EBS): green packets fit the committed allowance, yellow packets exceed CBS but fit EBS, and red packets exceed both. The RFC gives ingress policing as an example use where burst length, rather than peak rate, determines service eligibility.
sections.plainLanguage: The meter checks each packet against the configured rate and burst allowances. The marker writes the result as green, yellow or red in the packet's DS field.

sections.title: Configuration Parameters
sections.content:
An srTCM is configured with a mode, a Committed Information Rate (CIR), a CBS and an EBS. CIR is measured in bytes of IP packets per second, including the IP header but not link-specific headers. CBS and EBS are measured in bytes.

At least one of CBS or EBS must be greater than zero. The RFC recommends that each nonzero burst size be at least as large as the largest possible IP packet in the stream.
sections.plainLanguage: The CIR sets the rate at which tokens become available. CBS and EBS set the capacity of the two token buckets in bytes.

sections.title: How the Two Token Buckets Work
sections.content:
The Meter has two token buckets, C and E, with maximum sizes CBS and EBS. Both begin full and share the CIR. As tokens are added, bucket C fills first; bucket E receives a token only when C is full and E is not.

In Color-Blind mode, a packet uses tokens from C if it fits, otherwise from E if it fits, and is red if neither bucket has enough tokens for the whole packet. In Color-Aware mode, a packet's existing color also limits whether it can be marked green or yellow. An implementation need not use this exact internal model if its behavior is equivalent.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet uses tokens from the committed bucket when enough are available. Otherwise it may use excess-bucket tokens; if neither bucket can cover the packet, it is red.

sections.title: Writing the Color and Using It
sections.content:
The Marker sets the DS field to a codepoint that represents the Meter's result. With the Assured Forwarding per-hop behavior, color can be represented by the packet's drop precedence.

The RFC's example service discards red packets, forwards yellow packets as best effort and forwards green packets with a low drop probability. The document says the srTCM has no known security concerns.
sections.plainLanguage: A network can use the color to decide how to treat a packet. The example discards red packets, gives yellow packets best-effort service and gives green packets a lower drop probability.
